title: Reliability, rate limits & cost
summary: A model call is the slowest, most expensive and least reliable line in your service. This module measures and controls it: **tokens and cost** per request and per run, the provider's rate limit and your own, timeouts, retries, a fallback provider and a circuit breaker, routing easy requests to a cheaper model with per-caller budgets, and keeping abuse out with hashed API keys, plans and request limits.
learn: **Tokens and cost**: usage on every reply, estimating before sending, totals per run, a price table, runs with cost
**Rate limits**: InMemoryRateLimiter for the provider's, Redis for yours (per plan, per minute)
**When the provider fails**: timeouts, retries with backoff, a fallback provider, a circuit breaker
**The right model**: routing simple questions to a smaller model, cost per request, daily token budgets
**Keeping abuse out**: API keys stored as hashes, plans, 429 with Retry-After, request size limits
flow:
request ─→ API key (hash → plan) ─→ rate limit (Redis) ─→ budget left? ─→ route: small | default
   ─→ circuit breaker ─→ model (timeout, retries) ──fails──→ backup provider
   ─→ usage_metadata ─→ tokens × price ─→ cost per request, budget spent

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

path.title: Production path: the right model, priced, and still answering when a provider is down
path.summary: Simple questions go to the small model; each model sits behind a circuit breaker with Groq as backup; every request's tokens are priced from config and counted against the caller's daily budget; API keys are stored as hashes with a plan, and every plan has a per-minute limit in Redis.

steps.title: Route
steps.explain: route() sends questions with one part to the small model and the rest to the default; RoutedModel puts each behind a CircuitBreaker with the fallback provider.
production: Tune the rule on your own traffic: misrouted hard questions cost answers, not just money.

steps.title: Resilience
steps.explain: Timeouts and retries on every client (get_chat_model); with_fallback for a second provider; CircuitBreaker opens after circuit_threshold failures and skips the primary for circuit_cooldown_s.
production: Alert when the breaker opens: answers are coming from the backup, at its price.

steps.title: Limits
steps.explain: api_key matches sha256 hashes; rate_limited counts per caller per minute in Redis (429 + Retry-After); TokenBudget refuses a caller over today's tokens before any model call.
production: Without Redis the limits fail open, logged: decide per endpoint whether that's right.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.explain:
Ten support questions, five simple and five with several parts, through the default model alone and the routed setup, with Mistral up and down.

| | answered | right facts | latency p50 | US$ per 1,000 requests |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| default model only | 10/10 | 10/10 | 1.5 s | 0.026 |
| **routed, with fallback and breaker** | **10/10** | **10/10** | **2.6 s** | **0.020** |
| default model only · Mistral down | 0/10 | 0/10 | 2.6 s | — |
| **routed, with fallback and breaker · Mistral down** | **10/10** | **10/10** | **2.2 s** | **0.070** |

With Mistral down (an invalid key stands in for an outage), the default model alone answered nothing; the routed setup answered everything from Groq, and the breaker skipped the dead provider after two failures in a row instead of waiting on it for every request. With Mistral up, sending the five simple questions to the small model cut the cost per request by 22% with the same right facts. The backup costs more per request (reasoning tokens), so it's for outages, not every day. Prices are the example table in settings.model_prices.
production: Run the outage drill before every provider or model change.
